subject: chickenWalker
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: chicken-legged walking house-machine.
Style: Howl's Moving Castle.
reasoning:
I'm picturing a Howl's Moving Castle-inspired walking house: a jumbled cluster of cottages, turrets, chimneys, and balconies piled atop a riveted metal body, standing on two large chicken legs. Now I need to plan a solid TypeScript module using the SDK that renders this reliably without errors.

I'm working out the scale and proportions—roughly 7 meters total, with the legs taking up about 3 meters and the body 4 meters, plus a front "jaw" plate like teeth and glowing turret-window "eyes." Now I'm mapping out the actual rig: hips, knees, ankles, and toes for the chicken legs, positioning joints in 3D space starting from the hip coordinates.

For toes, I'll give each three forward digits plus a rear hallux, each a short chain of joints textured with scales and claw tips. Then I need to plan the main hull as the riveted house-body, roughly 3.2 wide and 2.2 tall, with hips tucked inside near the bottom, and figure out the root skeleton joint placement along with where the jaw attaches at the front.

For the skeleton hierarchy, I'll add a "cabin" joint above the hip root so the upper house cluster can sway independently, with legs, jaw, and toes branching off as their own role-tagged chains. Now I'm laying out the hull itself as a lofted shape running front to back with varying station widths.

For materials, I'm mixing a rusty, patched iron/copper look for the lower hull with weathered wood and plaster for the upper houses, echoing Howl's Moving Castle's rickety aesthetic. I'm checking whether the loft function supports a boxy cross-section option versus its default ellipse shape, since I want a blockier silhouette rather than smooth rounded panels.

For the face, I'm planning a protruding iron jaw with teeth spikes, an upper lip plate, and two cannon-like turret eyes with glowing yellow window decals, making sure the face reads clearly as the focal point. Then I'll build the upper cluster as a stack of small house-like boxes on top.

Setting up window glow intensity, then planning a house-building helper that assembles walls, gable roof, windows, and optional chimney, with manual yaw math for positioning elements accurately in rotated local frames rather than relying on part-local coordinates.

Designing the roof cross-section...

For walls, I'm planning half-timbered plaster texture with dark beam lines, stretched across each box face. For metal elements like turrets, barrels, and pipes, I'll use rusty iron, verdigris copper, and brass paints, and for chimneys I want custom brick patterns with caps plus a touch of puffy smoke cards standing upright.

For the smoke, four low-poly icosahedron puffs stacked upward above the main chimney will read better than flat cards. I'm also designing a round turret with stone or paneled copper cylinder walls, a cone roof with slate shingle texture, and a weathervane flag on top—possibly with a star emblem nodding to Calcifer.

That gives me an idea: a glowing porthole on the chest showing Calcifer's fire face as a drawn flame with eyes, giving the castle a signature feature. I'm also planning brass cannon barrels jutting from the sides, curved brass pipes with flange rings sweeping up the hull, and a hinged jaw at the front with an upper lip plate and lower jaw lined with iron teeth.

Now I'm adding two round turret eyes jutting forward like short cylinders, with glowing amber lenses, iron rims, and partial-sphere eyelid hoods to give the face a creature-like read, echoing Howl's castle's eye-window motif above the toothed mouth. For the legs, I'm thinking of a plump feathered drumstick shape in rusty orange tones leading into scaly yellow-orange lower legs, possibly with metal knee armor for that spindly, bird-like silhouette.

I'm detailing the shin and tarsus with painted scale bands plus a few brass cuffs for a mechanical touch, and feet with three front toes and a hallux, each segmented with dark claws. Feather cards scatter down the thigh leaning backward, with a feather "skirt" ring hanging around the hull's base — blending Howl's chicken-leg castle with the Baba Yaga hut image, pairing feathered thigh pants with scaly brass-cuffed legs below. Next I'm picturing a balcony with railing and a laundry line strung along one side.

I'm adding bunting flags strung between turrets using small triangle cards along a curve, skipping a propeller in favor of keeping scope tight, maybe adding a canvas sail instead. For the lower hull I'm placing rivets, a glowing hanging lantern, and a back door with a rope ladder. Budgeting parts to around 180-340 with roughly 60k triangles, now I'm working out the exact coordinates, starting with total height around 7.5m and placing the hip joint root position.

Now I'm calculating the hull loft dimensions and leg geometry, figuring out hip socket and foot target positions, segment lengths for thigh/shin/tarsus, and checking that the total reach can bridge the hip-to-foot distance with bending joints oriented like a chicken leg — knee forward, hock back.

Writing the leg chain function...

I'll crop the chain sweep using from/to ranges, splitting the leg into a thigh segment (fat drumstick, feather paint) and a shin/tarsus segment (scales), with slight overlap at the knee joint. The thigh radius tapers from hip to knee while shin and tarsus taper further down, and I need to check whether the thigh partly sits inside the hull since the hip point is near the hull's lower boundary.

I'll split the leg into a thigh sweep tapering from knee to hip with varying radius keys, then a shin sweep continuing to the foot, keeping round caps where they join. For the feet, I'm placing a tip joint at the foot point and spreading toes: three forward toes at angles plus a back hallux, each tapering in radius and resting flush against the ground plane.

Each toe follows a slightly arched path from the foot joint to its tip, with claws built as curved horn-colored spikes extending from each toe's end point down to touch the ground.

Now I'm adding flattened foot pad spheres that rest at ground level, then setting up the hip contact points and checking that all lowest points (pads and claw tips) sit near y=0. Next I'm defining the body hull by specifying cross-sections at various z positions along the spine, each with its own center height, width, and depth to shape the torso's silhouette front to back.

I'm thinking through how the loft between hull stations caps at the front and back—whether rounded or flat—since a flat octagonal front plate would give a nice surface to seat the face. I decide to use surface raycasting against the hull to precisely place the eyes and jaw rather than guessing coordinates, which is the proper way to seat features on a lofted shape.

For the ngon section, I realize the default orientation puts vertices at top/bottom and sides, making a diamond-like cross-section, so I switch to a flat-faced octagon with smooth disabled to get clean flat panels on top, bottom, and sides. Then I start planning the hull's paint treatment—panelled rusty metal mixing iron and copper tones with rust mottling, darker toward the lower band, using a custom paint function based on position and normal.

Now I'm figuring out where the deck sits on top of the hull's flat face, roughly at y≈4.95, and planning to attach a cabin joint there as the parent for all the deckhouses. I'm sketching out the first house in the cluster—a main cabin positioned slightly aft of center, with specific width, height, depth, and roof height, oriented to face forward.

Now I'm adding more houses to the cluster: a small front-left cabin angled at 20°, a taller back-right house angled the other way, and I'm debating whether to perch a tiny tilted house on top of the main roof for that classic Howl's Moving Castle chaotic stacking, even though it risks intersecting the roof slope.

Instead I'm opting for turrets — a round stone turret with a conical roof and flag on the back-right side, and a smaller onion-domed tower up front, plus brick and metal chimneys with smoke puffs on two of the houses.

Working through the vertex geometry, I find that at x=0.95 the hull's top surface sits around y=4.78 in world space, meaning a house with its bottom at 4.9 would float above the sloped edge by a noticeable margin. The fix is to make the house walls extend deeper, burying the bottom further into the hull around y=4.3.

For houses that sit outboard and overhang past the hull's edge, I'll let the overhanging portion hang free Howl's-castle-style, adding wooden support struts underneath for detail, while keeping most houses within the hull's width. Actually, a simpler approach: build a flat wooden deck platform on top of the hull, then place the houses on that deck instead of directly on the curved hull surface.

I'm placing the deck as a slightly overhanging box that sits on top of the hull's sloped surface, with strut brackets filling the gap under the overhanging edges, and setting the houses to rest on this deck's top surface. Now I'm working out the front hull cap geometry, considering an octagonal flat plate shape for the bow.

For the front face, I'm planning symmetric eye turrets as short cylinders protruding forward from the plate, each with an iron rim torus, a glowing lens disc, and a hooded eyelid formed from a partial half-cylinder shell slightly larger than the turret itself.

Above each eye I'm adding an angled brow plate for a determined expression, and designing the eye texture as an amber iris with dark pupil slit, ring lines suggesting a lens, and a glow boost for intensity. Below that, I'm laying out the mouth with an upper iron lip plate spanning across the front and hanging teeth spikes, with a lower jaw piece still to come.

Still placing jaw and teeth geometry...

I'm thinking I could make the mouth glow with Calcifer peeking from inside, like a little flame face glowing through the teeth gap for a fun detail. Now I'm sketching out the lip plate dimensions and position to sit just above the jaw.

Still blocking out geometry...

I should fill that gap with a little brass nose feature — maybe a stubby horn speaker or small riveted vent plate between the eyes, pointing forward. I'll settle on a brass bell-shaped nose via lathe, keeping it modest so it sits below the brow plates without crowding the eyes, and add slanted brow extrusions just above the eyes that poke slightly above the front plate's top edge in front of the deck.

Now I'm adding turret-style cannons on the hull sides, angled outward and forward with brass barrels and muzzle rings, plus a rear exhaust pipe, and sketching curved brass pipes running from the hull sides up into the deck using a Catmull-Rom spline path.

I'll also add twin backward-tilted smokestacks with flared lathe tops at the rear, puffs of smoke above them, a small balcony with railing on the left side of the main house, and a laundry line strung between the tower and house with hanging clothes cards.

Then I'm adding triangular bunting pennants strung from the tower to the chimney, glowing lanterns under the deck corners and near a door, and a short rope ladder hanging from the hull's underside at the back for charm. I'll also give the tower a weather vane with a wavy painted flag on top.

I'll make the flag emblem symmetric so orientation doesn't matter, with a swallowtail notch at the far end for the wave effect. For smoke puffs I'm considering flat icosahedron shapes in a light grey tone, and now I'm thinking through window textures for the card.

For windows I'm planning wooden-framed 4-pane variants glowing warm yellow, an arched style, and round portholes with brass rims for the hull, figuring out how to cast rays onto the hull surface to place each porthole decal flush against its normal.

Now I'm thinking about adding a horizontal belt band with rivets around the hull waist at y≈3.9, but realizing that height crosses the face plate near the upper lip, so I need to adjust where the loop runs to avoid conflicting with the face.

Actually, since the hull bottom at the front reaches y=3.2 while my plane is at y=3.1, the cutting plane stays under the face without touching the front plate—no slicing needed there. But I need to watch for the legs intersecting the hull bottom too, since the plane could cut multiple loops and I'd want the smallest one centered around that point.

For the band geometry itself, I'm sweeping along the loop with brass-colored hexagonal cross-section and placing bolt spheres at intervals around it. For a second band higher up at y=4.7, I need to check whether it clips the front plate (which starts around y=4.8), so I may need to slice that loop to avoid the collision, tracing the perimeter direction carefully from front-center rotating toward +X.

For the thigh surfaces, I'm planning a feather scatter of roughly 120 feather cards with sizes varying between 0.14 and 0.32, possibly with a feather skirt ring circling the hull near the bottom where it meets the thighs.

I'm sketching a feather SVG shape with a visible rachis line and two color variants—rust orange fading to dark brown tips, and a cream variant—for visual variety across the cards. For the toe scales, I'm planning a custom paint function using yellow-orange tones with scute ring patterns based on position along the leg sweep.

Writing scute ring logic...

I should add brass hock caps as mechanical knee joints with a cylinder axle, maybe a hydraulic piston rod along the shin bone for a cool mechanical detail, plus a rooster-like spur spike on the back of the tarsus.

Now I'm planning textures: a half-timbered plaster wall and a second painted clapboard wall variant.

I'm listing out the remaining textures — lit windows, arch and porthole glows, eye and Calcifer glows, feather variants, a flag, laundry/bunting pennants, and a door texture, bringing the count to about twelve. Then I'm thinking through paint materials: rusted hull metal panels, deck planks, slate and terracotta roofing, brick, chicken skin scutes, and brass/copper via a metal shader, plus stone tower plaster.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy — hips as root/spine, cabin spine, jaw, four joints per leg on each side, and three segments per toe across four toes per foot.

Writing helper functions for yaw rotation...

Writing house helper function...

I'll fix the knife-edge eave by adding a small fascia lip to the roof outline, and add a dark ridge cap rod spanning front to back. I also need to think through the gable end's coloring — since the roof prism's front/back triangular faces currently take the roof paint color, but the gable end should visually read as wall/timber instead.

For that, I'll build a roofPaint function that checks whether a face's normal aligns with the thickness axis — if so, it renders a timber board pattern (vertical stripes via UV coordinates) for the gable plaster look, otherwise it applies shingles. I'll also add a small round porthole window with a glow on the front gable face, placed using the yaw-oriented positioning helper.

Now I'm placing wall windows on the front face, spreading them evenly along x based on count, with side windows mirrored on the back face too for all-around viewing. I'm adding wooden sill boxes beneath each window and considering a small flower-box detail with red sphere clusters for charm, then moving on to the door plane with its texture.

Next I'm designing the chimney as a brick box with a darker cap slab, a pot cylinder, and smoke puffs on top, buried into the roof. For the tower, I'm building a cylindrical body with a cone roof, adding a shingle texture, overhang ring, finial spike, flagpole and flag, then working out how to place arched window planes around the faceted cylinder so they sit flush against its flat sides.

I'll design an "ashlar" stone paint pattern using row offsets based on angle, with warm grey tones for the tower and brick red for chimneys. For Howl's palette I'm thinking rusty browns, slate blue-grey roofs, cream walls, brass, glowing windows, verdigris touches, and maybe a pastel turquoise clapboard house for variety, then I'll start sketching the half-timber wall texture in SVG with a plaster background and dark timber beam framing.

Writing SVG code...

Adding more window variants...

Then a flag design with swallowtail notch, red field, yellow star, and white border, oriented along its length. For the laundry drawings, I'm sketching a striped shirt and sock, but need to account for the downstream view showing them upside-down, so the shirt's shoulders (normally at top) should align with the root edge at the bottom of the drawing.

For the pennant bunting, I'm making it a triangle with the wide edge at the drawing's bottom (root edge) and the apex pointing up, cycling through red, yellow, and teal textures via a randomized selection. The door design is a wooden arched door with iron hinges and a small round window, kept non-glowing, rounding out this set of card types alongside wall, clapboard, window, arch, porthole, and eye designs.

Counting up the full list - calcifer, feathers, flag, shirt, sock, three pennant colors, and door - that's 16 textures total, more than the suggested 5-12 range, but since this is just a profile it should still fit fine in a 4096 atlas at moderate 128-256 sizes per texture. I'm considering merging the three pennant colors into a single grayscale texture tinted by position using a paint function, so one base drawing could produce different colors depending on where it sits.

Now I want to lock down the exact API surface I'll be using - the part function with its various options like bone, position, rotation, texture, and scale, plus helpers like glow, cards, sweep, extrude, lathe, loft, surface raycasting, and decal - so I have the right calls ready before building the model.

All these come from the single "agentic-3js-builder" module, with specialized kits like clockwork and glow imported from their own subpaths. I'm confirming the paint functions return color values I can pass directly into part definitions.

Setting up the builder scaffold now, choosing a large paint texture size since the model's surface area needs finer detail resolution.

Checking the texel density math, I find rivets and seams at typical scale would end up sub-pixel, so I'll need to hand-roll a custom plate paint pattern at a coarser scale instead of using the default panelled function.

I'm sketching the joint hierarchy next, starting with a root body joint — thinking about whether to give it an explicit forward direction or leave it at identity orientation, and settling on naming it "hips" so rigging tools recognize it even though it represents a vehicle body.

Setting up the cabin and jaw joints relative to the hips, then building the leg joints symmetrically for left and right sides using hip and foot positions to define each limb's path.

Checking the geometry: hip-to-foot distance comes out to about 3.16 while the combined leg length is 3.55, so the leg does bend as expected. Working out where the knee lands, with the lower segment nearly vertical, the hock sits around (1.0, 1.17, 0.15), putting the hip-to-hock span near 2.11 against a thigh+shin total of 2.5, confirming forward knee flexion.

Now I'm placing the knee around (0.9, 2.3, 0.45) and checking the hock orientation — the shin runs backward-down from knee to hock while the tarsus runs forward-down from hock to foot, giving the hock a backward-pointing bend, which reads as a believable leg shape even if less exaggerated than a typical chicken hock.

Switching to using normalized parameters along the leg (tKnee, tHock) instead of exact coordinates, I'm computing the thigh's swept radius profile with tapering values and rounded end caps.

Now I'm defining the shin and tarsus as a radius function that tapers through the hock joint, then adding a brass disc cap to mark the hock joint where the shin tube is hidden under the fattened thigh.

I'm also sketching the hydraulic shin piston detail—a rod housing running behind the shin between the knee and hock, figuring out the perpendicular offset direction in the sagittal plane so it sits correctly behind the leg.

Adding brass cuffs around the tarsus with short tube segments, then placing a backward-pointing spur spike near the hock for a mechanical, leg-joint detail.

For the foot I'm sinking a scaled sphere pad slightly into the tarsus tip for contact, then setting up toe placement with splayed yaw angles and varying lengths for a natural claw spread.

Each toe gets a three-point curved path from the base through a knuckle arch to the tip, building a three-joint chain marked as a digit for the rig.

Attaching a tapered sweep for the toe shape and a small bezier claw at the tip with its own radius profile and bone, then checking the geometry so the claw and underside dimensions line up correctly, including adjusting the back toe's yaw offset for the left foot.

I'm skipping toe pads in favor of scute ring paint, then scattering feather cards across the thigh surface with size, lean, and bend parameters, adjusting the flow vector so the feathers drape downward like a drumstick, and planning a skirt ring of feather cards around the hull's bottom edge.

Now I'm adding a feather skirt scattered across the hull's underside wherever the normal faces downward, filtered to a specific x/z range so it reads as a shaggy, Baba Yaga-style feathered belly visible from low angles, with roughly 80 cards and dark mottled brown paint beneath. Then I'm starting to define the hull shape as a loft between positioned cross-sections with width and height parameters.

Still writing hull loft...

I'm double-checking whether `smooth` is a valid option on the loft/sweep call, since it might not be typed and could throw a TS error -- considering whether to drop it to reduce risk.

I'm working out the flat-face octagon geometry for the front plate dimensions, then plan to position eyes and mouth using raycasts against the hull surface to find accurate placement for the turret-style eyeballs.

Adding eye housing cylinder and brass rim...

I decide mirroring isn't needed for decals since pupils can just share the same symmetric texture with a top-left highlight on both eyes. For eyelids, I'm considering a curved hood shape over each eye, possibly using a partial cylinder to form the brow.

I'm designing an extruded crescent-shaped lid that sits above each eye, with its inner radius smaller than the lens radius so it occludes the top portion — giving a sleepy, half-closed, friendly look.

I want slight asymmetry for charm rather than anger, so I'm tilting the lid's lower edge so the outward side sits a touch higher than the inward side, using a small slope factor tied to the eye's side. Still mapping out the arc points for the outline to keep it from self-intersecting.

Still plotting lid outline points...

I'm checking that the lid only covers the top 30-40% of the eye, leaving the pupil visible below for a half-lidded, sleepy look. I'll give the lid a copper plating with small rivets placed along the front edge at regular intervals.

Now I'm working out the nose as a lathed brass horn between the eyes, shaping its hollow funnel profile to flare outward toward the front opening.

I'm checking for overlap between the nose and upper lip positions, adjusting the nose placement upward slightly to keep them visually distinct, then laying out the mouth geometry — an upper lip box plated in iron and a row of seven downward-pointing tooth spikes.

Now I'm adding the mouth cavity as a dark box behind the teeth, with a glowing plane positioned just in front of it to represent Calcifer's fire, then starting the jaw frustum geometry anchored at its joint point.

Teeth attach to the jaw bone so they'll move together, and I'm adding a brass chin bar along the jaw's front edge. Posing the jaw with a positive 9-degree rotation on the x-axis tips it down to open the mouth, so I need the jaw and teeth built before that pose is applied -- but now I'm second-guessing how the cavity interacts once the jaw is open.

Instead of a gauge on the face, I'll move it to the hull side near the front. I'm planning three portholes per flank with glowing circles and brass rim torus shapes, plus the belt bands, then turret mounts with hemisphere bases and barrels on each side of the hull.

Now I'm working out curving brass pipes that rise from the hull side up to the deck towers, using curved spline paths to connect the hull to tower T1.

I need to add flange rings along the pipe path by placing small torus shapes oriented to the tangent direction at intervals, using the frame option to orient each ring perpendicular to the pipe's travel direction.

Actually, a simpler approach is to just use short rods with larger radius at nearby points along the path to act as collars, attached to the cabin bone since both cabin and hips move together closely enough.

For the rear smokestacks, I'm placing two rods angling up from the back of the hull, giving them flared lathe tops and trailing smoke puffs. Then I'm laying out the deck as a plank-textured box sitting above the hull's face plate, checking it clears properly, and adding support brackets underneath the deck edges.

I'm calculating where the hull surface sits at each strut position by interpolating the hull's slope, then using a downward ray cast from above the deck edge to find the exact hit point on the hull surface so the diagonal struts connect cleanly from hull to deck underside.

Now I'm planning the deck's overall footprint and figuring out where railing posts should go versus where houses sit on top, mapping out the first house's position, dimensions, and roof ridge height.

Then I'm adding a second cottage-style house overlapping slightly with the first, a third taller plaster house with a slate roof overlapping the main house for a piled, clustered look, and a small cylindrical tower placed nearby.

I'm continuing with tower T2 topped by a copper onion dome, then planning a small dormer-like structure perched on the roof slope of H1 to add Howl's-style jumbled rooftop details, working out where it should sit relative to the main roof's rise.

Now I'm figuring out the roof geometry math so the dormer sinks properly into H1's slope without floating, then shifting to plan a laundry line stretched between the towers for a lived-in touch.

I'm routing the bunting string from T1's cone base down to T2's spire top, checking that its sag passes near H1's roof ridge without clipping it, then placing pennants along the curve.

Good, that clears the roofline. Now I'm adding chimneys: a brick box chimney C1 on H1's roof with a cap and rising smoke puffs, and a metal stovepipe C2 on H3 with a conical cap, sized to their respective roof heights. I'm placing four grey icosahedron puffs drifting upward and back from C1 to suggest smoke.

The overall model lands around 9 meters tall, which feels huge but fits the Howl's-moving-castle vibe for a walking house. I'm also thinking of adding a brass telescope sticking out from T2's window and a hanging lantern with a glowing box under the deck's front corners.

I'm working out the H1 door placement, fitting it visually between T2's tower and H2 so it stays unobstructed, with the door positioned at around x -0.3 just above ground level. I'm also considering whether to add a small porch roof or step stones near the entrance, plus another lantern by the door.

Now I'm figuring out window placement per house, since H2's roof height could block H1's front windows if placed too high against the shared wall. I'm simplifying by putting a single window above H1's door, with careful sizing to fit within the 1.15 wall height, and planning side windows separately on H1's unobstructed faces.

I need to check each face against the trees' footprints to avoid overlapping windows with foliage. T1 sits near x 0.4-1.3, z -1.3 to -0.4, which could overlap the left side and back of H1, while T2 and H3 affect the right and back faces similarly, so I'm placing windows at offset positions that clear these obstacles.

Given the complexity, I'll define an explicit windows list per house with face, u, v, and kind attributes, then write a helper to compute each window's local position based on which face it's on (front/back using lateral offset u, left/right using u as the z-offset).

For placement, I'm creating window panels with proper orientation so they stay upright regardless of which face they're on, then adding sills as thin boxes rotated to match the face's yaw so they sit flush against each wall.

I'm layering in flower boxes with small clustered spheres on some H2 windows, and adding shutters as paired boxes flanking windows on H1 and H3 for that charming Howl's-castle look, bringing each window to about four parts total. I'm also planning arched windows for the tower facets and considering a railing in front of the deck area, positioned above the lower face so it doesn't clash with the window layout.

Now I'm adding another railing along the deck's left edge near the clothesline, spacing posts evenly with thin connecting rails, and sketching out a hanging rope ladder from the hull's underside near the back, figuring out where it should attach based on the hull's bottom curve at different stations.

On the hull flanks, I'm placing a small gauge decoration with a needle near the front portholes, and considering adding a trio of small flat gears as a steampunk accent on the right flank between the porthole rows, oriented along the hull's curve.

Working out placement along z for each side face: left side gets portholes plus a gauge, right side gets portholes plus the gear train, with cannons mounted above on the upper slope. Since the hull tapers along z the side faces aren't flat, so I'll orient each part using the ray-hit normal rather than a fixed axis, and the gear train will need tinted textures for its colors.

Default tints should work fine for most parts, with the gear train placed slightly offset from the hit point along its normal and using the normal as its rotation axis. For materials I'm defining brass, copper, and iron presets with different tarnish/verdigris amounts and grain sizes, plus a custom rust-based hull paint that blends noise-driven base and fleck colors.

Writing rust streak and lighting logic...

Adding staggered seams and rivet details...

I should double check that `resolve` is properly exported from paint.ts since the clockwork kit imports it from the same package module.

Fixing the row modulo so negative rows don't break the plating pattern, then defining the hull using the plating function with rust base color. Now I'm writing the deck plank function that lays boards along z with randomized offsets per plank index, adding wood grain, dark seams, and nail dot details.

Now I'm starting a shingle roof paint generator that takes colors, edge style, mossiness, thickness, and gable color as parameters.

Still writing shingle shading logic... I'm also adding moss patches on upward-facing surfaces using noise, then double-checking that the ridge-aligned row coordinates still make sense for a gable roof's sloped planes.

For tower cones I need a different "along" coordinate based on angle around the axis rather than a straight row direction, so I'm planning to generalize the shingles function to accept a custom along-position function. I also want the underside of eaves to render as dark wood soffit instead of shingles, and for gable walls I'm sketching vertical timber board striping using the outline coordinates.

For nested paints, resolve() should fall back to the outer surface coordinates when none are passed, so boards painted inside another paint function still read the right position. Writing brick texture logic...

For the stone tower I'll compute ashlar rows by height bands and wrap the texture around the tower's angular position relative to its center axis, so I need a helper that takes the tower's center and radius. House walls use SVG textures while the tower uses procedural paint, and next I'm sketching the chicken-leg skin shader.

Writing scaly leg texture...

For the leg, I'm adjusting the chain parameter so scute rings follow the sweep length, and thinking through a mottled rust-and-dark feather underlayer for the thigh. For the tower's T2 body, I'm considering wrapping a clapboard SVG texture around the cylinder for the wooden board look.

I'm reconsidering T2 to use a flexible painted-wood texture with horizontal boards instead, maybe a blue-grey tint for variety against T1's stone. I'm also tallying up the wall textures needed—timber variants, clapboard, door, window, arch, portrait, eye, calc, feathers, flags, pennant, shirt, sock—landing around fifteen total texture types.

Now I'm thinking through smoke puffs using flat icosahedrons in muted cream tones, and adding a feather skirt along the hull's underside. I also need to design the rear of the hull: a big round hatch with a brass ring, iron disk, and wheel spokes, plus a rope ladder beneath it, positioned on the flat back cap facing outward.

I'm working through implementation pitfalls now: making sure bone assignments pass through explicitly for cabin, face, and card parts, and verifying the loft function's station array signature. I also need a helper function that safely handles raycasts against the hull surface, returning a fallback point and normal when the ray misses instead of crashing.

I'm also noting edge cases like the rng function returning a number generator, limb returning a Vector3 array that can double as a path, and the need to use non-null assertions for optional values like leg tips.

Then I move on to the paint function's typed parameters and unused argument handling, before working through geometry details for the tower body, roof cone, and window texturing, making sure UV mapping and faceted shading options line up with how paint interprets position and normal.

Next I design the onion dome using a lathe profile with a smoothed silhouette in verdigris copper, then add the finial spike and ball on top, followed by the flag assembly on tower one — a pole rising from the cone's tip with a ball and a card-based flag frame positioned near the pole's upper end.

Cards double-sided, with a small sink default so they root into the pole naturally.
